about: Phonics Practice, made by Teddy Rook Book to practice alongside Hannah Ward's lessons. Original word lists, sentences and stories. Checked by scripts/phonics/test.js.

teach-your-child-to-read.text: sounding out words, then the steps that follow

phonics-reading-boot-camp.text: all twelve steps, from letter sounds to longer words

steps.title: Letters and sounds
steps.blurb: Big and small letters, the sound each letter makes, and the first sound in a word.
steps.teaches: Every letter has a name (bee) and a sound (/b/). Reading starts with the sounds. This step practices matching big and small letters, finding the letter for a sound, and hearing the first sound in a word.

units.say: Short a, the sound at the start of apple. You can hold it: “aaa.”
Lips together, then a quick pop. Keep it short: /b/, not “buh.”
Here c says /k/, as in cat. Short and quiet, from the back of the mouth, with no “uh” after it.
Tongue taps behind the top teeth. Short: /d/, not “duh.”
Short e, the sound at the start of egg. You can hold it.
Top teeth on the bottom lip; let the air hiss out: “fff.”
Hard g, as in goat. Short, from the back of the mouth: /g/, not “guh.”
Just a short, quiet puff of breath.
Short i, the sound at the start of igloo. You can hold it.
Short: /j/ as in juice, not “juh.”
The same sound as c in cat. Short and quiet, no “uh.”
Tongue up behind the top teeth, and hold it: “lll.”
Lips together and hum: “mmm,” not “muh.”
Tongue up behind the top teeth; hum through the nose: “nnn.”
Short o, the sound at the start of octopus. Open wide; you can hold it.
Lips together, then a little puff of air. Short and quiet: /p/, not “puh.”
q nearly always comes with u. Together they say /kw/, as in quack.
Hold it: “rrr,” not “ruh.”
Like a snake: “sss.”
Tongue taps behind the top teeth with a little puff of air. Short: /t/, not “tuh.”
Short u, the sound at the start of umbrella. You can hold it.
Top teeth on the bottom lip, and buzz: “vvv.”
Round your lips, then open them. Keep it short: /w/, not “wuh.”
x usually says /ks/, the sound at the end of fox.
The sound at the start of yarn. Keep it short: /y/, not “yuh.”
Buzz like a bee: “zzz.”

offscreen: Sing the alphabet song while you point to each letter on a chart.
Play “I spy something that starts with /m/.” Say the sound, not the letter name.
Trace letters in a tray of salt or sand, or make them from play dough, saying the sound as you go.
Match magnetic letters: a big A with a small a.
steps.hannah: Goes with Hannah's Crystal and Shell Pre-Reading Workbook and her Teach Your Child the Alphabet in 60 Lessons. Do her lesson first, then a few minutes here with the letters your child has met.
steps.tip: Say each sound short and clear. Hold the sounds you can hold (mmm, sss, fff); keep the others crisp, with no “uh” after them.

steps.title: Short vowels
steps.blurb: The five short vowel sounds, as in apple, egg, igloo, octopus and umbrella.
steps.teaches: The vowels a, e, i, o and u are in nearly every word. Here they make their short sounds. Your child listens for the middle sound of a short word (c-a-t) and finds its vowel.

units.say: Short a, as in apple. Hold it: “aaa.”
Short e, as in egg. Hold it: “eee” (the e in egg, not the e in eat).
Short i, as in igloo. Hold it: “iii.”
Short o, as in octopus. Mouth wide open: “ooo” (the o in on).
Short u, as in umbrella. Hold it: “uuu” (the u in up).

offscreen: Say a short word slowly (c-aaa-t) and ask, “What sound is in the middle?”
Make up a silly chant for each vowel: “a, a, apple.”
Point to the vowels in a book title or a cereal box together.
steps.hannah: Short vowels come early in Hannah's Teach Your Child to Read in 120 Lessons and in her Phonics Reading Boot Camp. Practice here once your child has met the vowels in her lessons.
steps.tip: The short vowel sounds are the ones in apple, egg, igloo, octopus and umbrella. They can be held a little; that makes them easy to hear.

steps.title: Sound it out
steps.blurb: Blend three sounds into a word: tap each sound, then slide to say it fast.
steps.teaches: Blending is the heart of reading: say each sound in order, then run them together into a word. These are three-sound words with a short vowel in the middle (cat, sit, mop). Your child taps each sound box, saying the sound, then slides a finger under the word and says it fast.
sentences: The cat is on a mat.
A big pig sat in the mud.
Sam can hop to the bus.
Is the red hen in the pen?
I got a hat.
Tim had a hot bun.

stories.title: A Pup in the Sun
lines: The pup dug in the mud.
The pup is in the tub!
The pup can nap in the sun.

stories.title: Dot Hid
lines: Dot the hen hid in a box.
A fox sat on a log.
The fox did not get Dot!

offscreen: Use three cups or sticky notes, one letter each. Touch each one as you say its sound, then sweep your finger under them and say the word.
Play “robot talk”: say a word in sounds (/p/ /i/ /g/) and let your child say it fast (pig). Then swap.
Hold the sounds you can hold so they run together: “mmmaaat” is easier to blend than separate sounds.
steps.hannah: Goes with Hannah's Teach Your Child to Read in 120 Lessons once your child is sounding out short words there, and with the first part of Phonics Reading Boot Camp.
steps.tip: Tap and say each sound, then slide and say the word fast. If a word comes out choppy, say it again with the sounds held and joined.

steps.title: Word families
steps.blurb: Words that rhyme and share an ending: cat, hat, sat. Also ll, ss, ff and zz.
steps.teaches: A word family is a group of words with the same ending, like -at (cat, hat, sat) or -ig (big, dig, pig). Changing only the first sound makes a new word. This step also brings in doubled letters at the end of short words: bell, kiss, puff, buzz. The two letters make one sound.

units.say: Two f's, one sound: “fff,” as in puff.
Two l's, one sound: “lll,” as in bell.
Two s's, one sound: “sss,” as in kiss.
Two z's, one sound: “zzz,” as in buzz.

sentences: A fat cat sat on a hat.
Ten men met a hen.
Bill can sell a big bell.
Did the bug buzz?
Was the pup on the hill?
Pass the jam to Dad.

stories.title: The Bun on the Hill
lines: Gus sat on top of the hill.
A pup ran up the hill.
Gus fed the pup a bit of bun.

stories.title: A Big Mess
lines: Pip had mud on his leg.

offscreen: Write a family ending (-at) on a card. Hold letter cards in front of it, one at a time, and read each new word.
Rhyme in the car: “What rhymes with hop?” Silly words count too, as long as they rhyme.
Fold a paper strip so only the first letter changes, like a flip book.
steps.hannah: Pairs with the rhyming and word-reading parts of Hannah's 120 lessons. Use it as extra practice when a lesson brings in words that rhyme.
steps.tip: Read the ending first (-at), then put the first sound on: /k/ ... at, cat. Changing just one sound makes a new word.

steps.title: Build words
steps.blurb: Spell short words with letter tiles: hear the sounds, then find the letters.
steps.teaches: Building words is blending turned around. Your child says a word slowly, hears each sound, and picks the letter for it. Spelling this way makes reading stronger, because it uses the same sounds and letters.
sentences: We can fix the box.
He did not get wet.
Go to bed, Ben!
Do not let the dog dig.
So we sat in the sun.
Can you hug me?

stories.title: A Hut in a Box
lines: Dad cut a gap in the box.
He can get in the hut.
He can nap in the hut.
He will not rip the hut.

stories.title: Go, Bug, Go
lines: A red bug is on a log.
The bug sat on the log.
So Kit sat. The bug sat.

offscreen: Say a word slowly and let your child pick magnetic letters for each sound.
Hold up one finger for each sound in a word (c-a-t is three fingers), then find the letters.
Write the word together on paper or in salt, saying each sound as you write its letter.
steps.hannah: Goes with the writing and spelling practice in Hannah's 120 lessons and her Little House Kindergarten. Building words here is extra practice, not a replacement for writing by hand.
steps.tip: Say the word slowly with your child and stretch the sounds: “mmm-ooo-p.” Let them find the letter for each sound, left to right.

steps.title: Two letters, one sound
steps.blurb: sh, ch, th, wh, ck and ng: two letters that make one sound.
steps.teaches: Some pairs of letters make one new sound: sh (ship), ch (chick), th (bath), wh (whale), ck (sock) and ng (ring). These pairs are called digraphs. In the sound boxes they share one box, because they are one sound. nk (bank) comes along with ng.

units.say: Finger to your lips: “shhh.” Two letters, one sound.
A short, quick sound, like a little sneeze: /ch/, not “chuh.”
Tongue peeks out between the teeth. th has two sounds, as in thin and this. Both are right.
Most Americans say wh just like w, as in whale.
Two letters, one sound: /k/. ck comes right after a short vowel, as in sock.
A hum at the back of the mouth, as at the end of ring. You can hold it.
n before k says /ng/, so nk sounds like the end of bank.

sentences: The fish is in the dish.
Chip the chick sat on a rock.
I wish I had a ship.
Sing a long song with me.
When will they get back?
She put a pink sock on.

stories.title: The Pink Shell
lines: She got it on a rock.
Beth put the shell in a box.
Then she put the box in a sock.
“What is in the sock?” said Josh.
“Is it a fish? Is it a chick? Is it a ring?”

stories.title: Quack!
lines: A duck sat on the dock.
“Can I sit with you?” said the chick.
Then they had a nap in the sun.

offscreen: Go on a sound hunt: find things at home with sh, ch or th (shoe, chair, bath).
Write sh, ch and th on three cards. Say a word and let your child hold up the right card.
Remind your child: when two letters make one sound, tap them together.
steps.hannah: Practice here after sh, ch, th and the rest have come up in Hannah's 120 lessons or her Phonics Reading Boot Camp. Her lessons set the order; use the cards for the sounds she has taught.
steps.tip: Two letters, one sound: tap the pair once. If your child says /s/ /h/ for sh, cover the h and uncover it: “Together they say shhh.”

steps.title: Blends
steps.blurb: Two or three consonants side by side, each still heard: frog, stop, hand, jump.
steps.teaches: In a blend, two or three consonants sit side by side and you still hear each one: fr in frog, st in stop, nd in hand, mp in jump. Each letter keeps its own sound box. Blends make words longer, so slow, steady tapping helps.
sentences: The frog can jump in the pond.
Stop the truck!
Brad has a red flag.
We swim in the pond and rest on the sand.
I have a gift from Gran.
Come and help me plant this.

stories.title: The Frog on the Log
lines: A frog sat on a log in the pond.
Snap! The frog got the bug.
The frog did not stop to chat.
Splash! He hid in the pond.
The frog got back on his log.
He had a nap in the hot sun.

stories.title: A Tent in the Grass
lines: Fred and his dad have a tent.
They set it up in the grass.
Fred got a lamp, a snack and a pad.
Fred and Dad rest in the tent.

offscreen: Say a blend word with a pause, “s...top,” and let your child put it together.
Make two piles of letter cards, a blend (st, fr, cl) and an ending (-op, -og, -ap), and see how many real words you can make.
Clap or tap for each sound in a blend word: s-t-o-p is four taps.
steps.hannah: Goes with the longer words in the middle of Hannah's 120 lessons and her Phonics Reading Boot Camp. If her lesson for today had blends, practice the same kind here.
steps.tip: Every letter in a blend keeps its own sound. Tap each one, then slide. If one gets dropped (sop for stop), tap the blend again slowly.

steps.title: Final e
steps.blurb: A silent e at the end makes the vowel say its name: cap and cape, kit and kite.
steps.teaches: When a word ends in vowel-consonant-e, the e is silent and the vowel says its name (its long sound): cap becomes cape, kit becomes kite, hop becomes hope, cub becomes cube. In the sound boxes, the vowel and the e are joined by a line.

units.say: The e at the end is silent. It makes a say its name, as in cake.
The silent e makes i say its name, as in kite.
The silent e makes o say its name, as in bone.
The silent e makes u say its name, as in cube. In some words it says /oo/, as in flute.
The silent e makes e say its name, as in these. It is the least common of the five.

sentences: Jake ate a big cake.
I like to ride a bike.
The snake is in the hole.
Can you fix the kite?
Where is the bone?
Take one plate, not two.

stories.title: The White Kite
lines: It was white with a red stripe.
Up, up, up went the kite!
It rose up to the sun.
Then the kite fell in a pine.
Kate gave the line a tug.

stories.title: The Cave
lines: Mike and Jane hike to a cave.
The cave is wide and still.

offscreen: Write cap, kit, hop and cub on cards. Add a sticky note with e and read the new word: cape, kite, hope, cube.
Read pairs aloud together: mad and made, pin and pine, not and note.
Point out that the e at the end is silent: it doesn't get a sound box of its own.
steps.hannah: Goes with the long-vowel words in the later part of Hannah's 120 lessons and her Phonics Reading Boot Camp.
steps.tip: Before sounding out, look at the end of the word. A vowel, one consonant, then e: the vowel says its name and the e stays quiet.

steps.title: Vowel teams
steps.blurb: ai, ay, ee, ea, oa, ow and igh: vowel teams that say a long sound.
steps.teaches: A vowel team is two or three letters that work together to make one long vowel sound: ai and ay (rain, play), ee and ea (bee, leaf), oa and ow (boat, snow), igh (light). Each team shares one sound box. y at the end of a short word says long i (my, fly).

units.say: ai says long a, as in rain. It is usually in the middle of a word.
ay says long a, as in play. It usually comes at the end of a word.
ee says long e, as in bee.
ea usually says long e, as in leaf. (In a few words, like head, it says short e; those come later.)
oa says long o, as in boat.
ow can say long o, as in snow. Later it will also say /ow/, as in cow.
igh says long i, as in light. The g and h are silent.
y at the end of a short word says long i, as in my and fly.

sentences: The sheep sleep by the green tree.
Can you see the boat on the sea?
It might rain, so bring a coat.
Play with me in the snow!
A bee is on my leaf.
Why does the goat eat my hat?

stories.title: A Gray Day
lines: They paint a green tree and a red train.
Then the rain stops, and the sky is bright.
Jay and Neal go and play.
They sail a leaf boat in the stream.
“This is the best day,” said Jay.

stories.title: The Goat and the Coat
lines: A goat sat by the road.
A man came by in a coat.
Then the man got a peach.
He gave the goat the peach.
The goat let go of the coat.
From then on, the man kept a peach with him.

offscreen: A saying many families use: “When two vowels go walking, the first one does the talking.” It works for ai, ee, ea and oa, though not for every word, so treat it as a hint.
Sort word cards into piles by sound: the long a pile (rain, play), the long e pile (bee, leaf), and so on.
Look for vowel teams on signs and packages when you are out.
steps.hannah: Goes with the vowel teams in the second half of Hannah's 120 lessons and in her Phonics Reading Boot Camp.
steps.tip: Find the team first and frame it with two fingers. The team is one sound box: r-ai-n.

steps.title: Vowels with r
steps.blurb: ar, or, er, ir and ur: an r after a vowel changes the vowel's sound.
steps.teaches: When r comes right after a vowel, it changes the vowel's sound: ar (car), or (corn), and er, ir and ur, which all say the same sound (her, bird, turtle). These are called r-controlled vowels. Each pair shares one sound box.

units.say: ar says the sound in car and star.
or says the sound in corn and fork.
er says the sound in her. Hold it: “errr.”
ir says the same sound as er, as in bird.
ur says the same sound as er, as in turtle.

sentences: The car is in the barn.
A bird sat on the fern.
Turn left at the farm.
Her shirt has a star on it.
Is this your fork?
Many stars shine at night.

stories.title: The Storm
lines: It is dark on the farm.
A storm is on the way.
Burt and Fern run to the barn.
The hens and the pig are in the barn.
The hens hide in the corn.
Fern and Burt sit on the hay.
They wait for the storm to stop.
The sky is bright with stars.

stories.title: Bart and the Horn
lines: The dog hides in the barn.
“Play it in the park,” she said.
In the park, Bart plays for the ducks.

offscreen: Say pairs and listen for the change: cat and cart, fin and firm, hut and hurt.
Make a “bossy r” card and lay it after a vowel card. Read the vowel, then read it with the r.
Hunt for ar, or and er words in a favorite picture book.
steps.hannah: Goes with the r-controlled vowels in the later lessons of Hannah's 120-lesson program and her Phonics Reading Boot Camp.
steps.tip: er, ir and ur sound the same. When your child spells, they'll need to learn which one a word uses; when reading, any of them says “er.”

steps.title: More vowel sounds
steps.blurb: oo (moon, book), ou and ow (cloud, cow), oi and oy (coin, toy), aw and au (paw, launch).
steps.teaches: These vowel pairs make sounds that are not long or short: oo has two sounds (moon and book), ou and ow say /ow/ (cloud, cow), oi and oy say /oi/ (coin, toy), and aw and au say /aw/ (paw, launch). Usually oi and ou come inside a word, and oy and ow at the end.

units.say: oo says /oo/, as in spoon.
oo can also say the short sound in book. If one sound doesn't make a real word, try the other.
ou says /ow/, as in cloud: the sound you make when you bump your knee.
ow can say /ow/, as in cow. (It can also say long o, as in snow.)
oi says /oi/, as in coin.
oy says /oi/ too, as in toy. It usually comes at the end of a word.
aw says /aw/, as in paw. In much of America it sounds like the o in hot; either is fine.
au says the same sound as aw, as in launch.

sentences: The cow is in the brown barn.
Look at the moon!
Roy has a toy boat.
The owl says, “Hoot!”
We found a coin in the soil.
Draw a cat with a big paw.

stories.title: The Owl Book
lines: Joy took a book to her room.
It was a book on owls.
Joy sat down on the rug and read.
They hoot, and they fly with no sound.
It sat on a branch by her room.

stories.title: The Brown Cow
lines: A brown cow stood by a pool.
A boy came down the road with a pail.
Then she let him fill the pail.
The boy gave the cow some hay.
Now the cow is his friend.

offscreen: Make the sounds with actions: “ow” as if you bumped your knee, “oi” like a pirate's “ahoy,” “aw” as if you saw a puppy.
For oo, read the word both ways (moon and book) and ask which one is a real word.
Sort cards by sound: all the /ow/ words in one pile, whether they use ou or ow.
steps.hannah: Goes with the last part of Hannah's 120 lessons and her Phonics Reading Boot Camp, where these vowel sounds come in.
steps.tip: oo has two sounds and ow has two sounds. Teach your child to try one, and if it isn't a real word, try the other.

steps.title: Endings and longer words
steps.blurb: -s, -es, -ed and -ing, and two-syllable words like sunset and rabbit.
steps.teaches: Endings change a word: cat to cats, wish to wishes, jump to jumped and jumping. Find the base word first, then add the ending. -ed can say /t/ (jumped), /d/ (filled) or /ed/ (landed). Longer words are read in parts called syllables: sun-set, rab-bit, pump-kin. Each part has one vowel sound. y at the end of a longer word says long e (happy).

units.say: -s means more than one (cats) or is part of a verb (he hops). It says /s/ or /z/ (cats, dogs).
-es is added after s, x, z, sh and ch. It adds a beat: box, box-es.
-ed means it already happened. It says /t/ (jumped), /d/ (filled) or /ed/ (landed).
-ing means it is happening. A short word with a short vowel doubles its last letter first: run, running.
y at the end of a longer word says long e, as in happy and puppy.

sentences: The rabbit hopped in the garden.
We had a picnic at sunset.
Mother is baking muffins.
The kittens are playing with a basket.
My brother jumped in the water.
People rested on the sandy hill.

stories.title: The Pumpkin Picnic
lines: Ted and his brother planted a pumpkin.
At last it was as big as a bathtub!
Then the people on the street came for a picnic.
They had muffins and milk at sunset.

stories.title: The Lost Kitten
lines: It was hiding, and it was crying.
At last she spotted a tail sticking up.
It was the kitten, napping in a basket!

offscreen: Cover the ending with a finger, read the base word, then uncover the ending: jump, jumped.
Clap the syllables of names and words: Sat-ur-day, pump-kin, rab-bit.
Write a two-syllable word on a card, cut it between the syllables, and read each half, then the whole.
steps.hannah: Goes with the end of Hannah's 120 lessons and her Phonics Reading Boot Camp, and leads into the reading in her American Pioneer Level 1.
steps.tip: Find the base word first, then add the ending. For a longer word, read one part at a time, then put the parts together.
